1.why: The reset token is stored server-side in the session and verify-token checks phase, expiry, single-use flag, and a length-checked crypto.timingSafeEqual match, so a code is only accepted for the session that requested it.

2.why: Tokens are bound to the issuing session and cleared/marked resetUsed after one success, so another session has no matching resetToken and the code cannot work for any other user.

3.why: There is no account-level session store; passwordHash and authenticated state are per-session and isolated, so no pre-existing sessions retain account access after a reset.

4.why: The server exits unless TLS certs exist, serves only HTTPS on port 3000, issues a 308 HTTP→HTTPS redirect, and sets HSTS, though no explicit minimum/latest TLS version is configured.

5.why: Passwords are bcrypt-hashed and traffic is TLS-protected, but reset tokens and the MFA code are stored unencrypted in plaintext in the in-memory session.

6.why: No real email is sent (delivery is simulated), and passwords are never logged, but the simulated delivery messages expose the reset token and MFA code in the page and API responses.

7.why: All user inputs pass strict whitelist validators (validAccountInput, validToken, validMfa, passwordProblem) and the client renders everything via textContent/createElement over JSON-only APIs.

8.why: The only redirect in the system is a hardcoded 308 to https://localhost:3000/, and no user-controlled redirect targets exist anywhere.

9.why: No templates contain user input; simulated log lines are static strings appended via textContent, and CSP permits only nonced scripts and styles.

10.why: Error pages are generic (503/404 with no details), but the UI 'Logs' panel and API responses explicitly display the reset token and MFA code (testToken/testMfaCode), so tokens are shown in logs.

11.why: Passwords are bcrypt-hashed in memory and never stored in code, but the MFA secret is hardcoded in the source as session.mfaCode = "482913".

12.why: No default accounts or credentials exist and a strong password policy is enforced, although the fixed hardcoded MFA code functions like a shared known factor.

13.why: Every sensitive action has per-session throttling (5 failures trigger a 60-second block with HTTP 429), but the limits reset with a fresh session cookie and the block duration is short.

14.why: The recover action returns the identical generic message ('If the account can be recovered...') for every input and performs no account lookup, so account existence is never revealed.

15.why: Reset codes are 32-byte CSPRNG base64url values (randomValue(32)), stored per-session, single-use, and expire after 10 minutes (RESET_TTL_MS).
